title: Out among the planets, and home again
audience: Curious adults sharing a visit with their 80-year-old grandparents; warm, conversational narration with no assumed astronomy knowledge or assumptions about ability.
introduction: Welcome aboard. I'm glad we're taking this trip together. We'll head out among the planets, collect a few good stories, and come home again. There's time to look around. The universe can wait a moment.

stops.subject: Sun
stops.objective: Connect the Sun's unfamiliar scale and fusion to the warmth of ordinary life.
stops.narration: Let's begin with the star we know best. The Sun can seem so ordinary that we forget what it is. Deep inside, hydrogen nuclei join together to make helium, releasing the energy that eventually shines out into space. Some of that energy warms your face on a sunny afternoon. I rather like that connection: all this astonishing physics, and at the other end, a pleasant spot to sit.
cameraIdeas: Keep the whole Sun comfortably inside the frame and slowly widen during the narration.
After the last sentence, hold the view silently for minimumViewSeconds before traveling onward.

stops.subject: Venus
stops.objective: Use Venus's reverse rotation and thick atmosphere to make a familiar-looking neighbor surprising.
stops.narration: Now Venus, our dazzling evening or morning companion. She's nearly Earth's size, but she keeps a very different household. Her thick atmosphere traps enough heat to melt lead at the surface. And Venus spins the opposite way from Earth: if you could see through those clouds, the Sun would rise in the west. Even sunrise, something that feels utterly dependable at home, has other arrangements out here.
cameraIdeas: Ease around Venus toward a crescent while keeping the complete globe in frame.
Hold the crescent silently for minimumViewSeconds after the narration.

stops.subject: Moon
stops.objective: Give the Moon a human connection through the Apollo tracks and the lack of weather that would erase them.
stops.narration: Before we head farther out, here's our Moon. Think of the Apollo astronauts trying out their first awkward steps in that powdery ground. Their tracks linger because there's no wind or rain to sweep them away. Lunar orbiters have photographed the trails they left. A walk on a beach disappears with the tide; a walk here can become part of the landscape's long memory. Let's stay with that thought for a moment.
cameraIdeas: Make a slow, shallow orbit around the Moon with the boundary between day and night crossing the globe.
Keep the framing broad; the story does not require Apollo sites or tracks to be visible. Hold silently for minimumViewSeconds afterward.

sources.title: NASA Science: 10 cool things NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter is teaching us about the Moon

stops.subject: Mars
stops.objective: Explain how rounded pebbles let scientists recognize an ancient stream on Mars.
stops.narration: Mars has a story hidden in something wonderfully modest: pebbles. The Curiosity rover found rounded stones cemented into ancient rock. Flowing water had rolled and worn them, just as a stream smooths stones on Earth. Imagine standing beside that Martian stream long ago, hearing water over the gravel. We don't know whether anything ever lived there. But we can recognize a place where water once ran, from the shape of a stone.
cameraIdeas: Fly a little closer to Mars during the narration, maintaining a view of the whole globe.
Let the camera settle for minimumViewSeconds of silence; do not target individual stones or imply an ancient stream is rendered.

sources.title: NASA JPL: Evidence about a Martian streambed

stops.subject: Jupiter
stops.objective: Tell how repeated observations of Jupiter's moons challenged the idea that everything circles Earth.
stops.narration: At Jupiter, a few little lights helped change our place in the universe. In sixteen ten, Galileo noticed points of light beside this planet. He kept looking, night after night. They changed places, but stayed with Jupiter. They were moons circling another world. Everything in the heavens couldn't be circling Earth after all. Picture him returning to that small telescope, notebook ready, wondering where tonight's dots would be.
cameraIdeas: Orbit Jupiter slowly during the account of Galileo's observations, then widen to give the planet room in the surrounding sky.
Hold silently for minimumViewSeconds. The narration does not depend on any moon being resolved in this composition.

sources.title: NASA: 410 years ago, Galileo discovers Jupiter's moons

stops.subject: Saturn
stops.objective: Let Saturn's appearance lead into the physical reality of its rings.
stops.narration: Ah, Saturn. Let's give this one a little room. Those rings look almost too tidy to be real, like someone has carefully set the planet into a piece of jewelry. Yet they're made mostly of countless pieces of water ice, all traveling around Saturn. From a distance, all those separate journeys become this graceful shape. I could happily linger here. We will, for a few quiet seconds.
cameraIdeas: Widen until Saturn and its main rings fit comfortably, then gently change the viewing angle to open the ring ellipse.
Continue only a very slow orbit during minimumViewSeconds of silence; stay outside the rings and do not resolve individual particles.

stops.subject: Neptune
stops.objective: Make Neptune's mathematical discovery understandable as a prediction tested by a telescope.
stops.narration: Our farthest stop is Neptune, a planet with a marvelous entrance. Astronomers noticed that Uranus wasn't quite following its predicted path. Could another planet be tugging on it? The mathematician Le Verrier worked out where to look. In eighteen forty-six, Galle found Neptune on his first night of searching. A calculation on paper had pointed toward a whole unseen world. That's a very satisfying piece of detective work.
cameraIdeas: Approach Neptune slowly, then ease into a shallow orbit with the globe surrounded by open sky.
Hold the settled composition silently for minimumViewSeconds before returning to Earth.

stops.subject: Earth
stops.objective: Return home through Voyager's Pale Blue Dot photograph and leave space for personal reflection.
stops.narration: And here we are, back at Earth. In nineteen ninety, Voyager One looked homeward and photographed our planet as a tiny point of light: the Pale Blue Dot. After visiting these other worlds, that picture feels especially dear. Somewhere on this globe are the streets you know, the people you're fond of, and the place you'll sleep tonight. Let's enjoy seeing our own planet as a destination.
cameraIdeas: Return to a broad, gently lit Earth composition and orbit slowly without trying to reproduce Voyager's historical position.
After the narration, rest on Earth for minimumViewSeconds of silence, then speak the closing without moving away.

sources.title: NASA Science: Voyager 1's Pale Blue Dot

closing: Thank you for coming along. We can stay here a while, or go back to whichever world has left you with a question. Saturn is awfully tempting.
